prompt.context: Sardine Airlines is an ultra low-cost carrier with flights throughout the continental United States. They have hub airports in Oakland, California; Tulsa, Oklahoma, and Hartford, Connecticut. Sardine Airlines is facing increased pressure from other low cost carriers such as Cattle Car Air and Soul Airlines. Sardine Airlines has faced declining profit for the past year. Sardine's CEO, Penny McPincher, has asked your team for advice on how to reverse the profitability trend.
prompt.question: How can Sardine Airlines reverse its declining profitability trend? The CEO is targeting a profit margin of 20% (net income / total revenue).

clarifying_info.a: Sardine Airlines competes primarily on having the lowest cost fares and offering minimal service. Due to its business model, Sardine Airlines has a culture of cost savings that can be passed to the customer.

clarifying_info.q: What is the profit margin target?
clarifying_info.a: Sardine Airlines is trying to grow profit margin to 20% (net income / total revenue).

clarifying_info.q: Can you share revenue and cost data?
clarifying_info.a: [Give the candidate Exhibit 1, Statement of Operations]
Non-ticket revenue includes things like bag fees, food, beverages, customer service charges, paper tickets, etc.
Landing fees are what Sardine Airlines pays to use airports.

exhibits.title: Statement of Operations
exhibits.shows: Multi-year income statement (2012-2015) showing passenger revenue, non-ticket revenue, total revenue, and operating expenses broken down by fuel, landing fees, maintenance, SG&A, and special charges, leading to net income before and after taxes. All figures in millions (unaudited).

framework: Structure the problem as Revenues vs. Costs
Revenue: analyze passenger and non-ticket revenue trends and growth rates
Costs: break down each cost line as a % of total revenue and identify which lines are growing disproportionately
Identify the primary profitability driver — SG&A increasing from 15% to 20% of revenue
Quantify the gap to target: 20% margin requires net income of $428.6M; current net income is $371M, gap is ~$57.6M
Drill into SG&A components to find actionable cost levers
Evaluate maintenance cost trend with context from regulatory environment
Develop recommendations to close the $57.6M gap

questions.prompt: Analyze Exhibit 1. What trends do you observe, and what is the primary driver of declining profitability?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will: (1) note total revenue has grown each year (4% YoY in 2015, 16% in 2014); (2) observe passenger revenue was nearly flat in 2015 (-0.37%) while non-ticket grew 9%; (3) identify that SG&A as % of revenue jumped from 15% (2014) to 20% (2015), the largest proportionate increase among expense lines; (4) note maintenance costs also rose proportionately (4% in 2012 to 10% in 2015); (5) conclude SG&A is the primary driver of profit decline.

math.setup: Target margin = 20%. Target net income = 20% x $2,143M = $428.6M. Current net income = $371M. Gap = $428.6M - $371M = $57.6M.
math.answer: Sardine Airlines needs to increase net income by approximately $57.6M to hit the 20% margin target.

questions.prompt: [Give candidate Exhibit 2 - SG&A Breakdown after they identify SG&A as the key driver.] What is driving SG&A growth and what should the company focus on?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates identify the three largest absolute YoY increases: Customer Service (+$52M), Rent (+$40M), and Marketing (+$24M). They note Salaries ($+1M) and Miscellaneous ($+2M) are immaterial. They focus on Customer Service and Rent as the actionable levers given the CEO/Board's position on marketing.

math.setup: YoY absolute changes in SG&A line items from 2014 ($309M) to 2015 ($428M).
math.answer: Customer Service ($52M) and Rent ($40M) are the two largest and most actionable cost drivers, together accounting for $92M of the $119M SG&A increase.

questions.prompt: [Give candidate Exhibit 3 - FAA memo if they raise maintenance costs.] What does this tell you about the maintenance cost trend?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates recognize that the FAA memo indicates Sardine Airlines was previously under FAA maintenance supervision due to insufficient maintenance standards. The increase in maintenance spending is a corrective investment to meet safety standards, not an inefficiency. Candidates should move away from recommending maintenance cuts.

questions.prompt: Given the context from Prompt 2, what specific recommendations would you make to address the SG&A issues around rent and customer service?
questions.guidance: Rent: The firm does not have to be headquartered in Oakland but wants to be where it has major operations. Rent in Tulsa or Hartford would be 40% less than 2015 Oakland rent. The $40M rent increase was driven by the Oakland landlord raising rent by $35M. Relocating HQ to Tulsa or Hartford saves $34.4M (40% of $86M current rent). Customer Service: Call center complaints surged ~3,000% due to 12-inch seat installation. Current vendor bills 60% more because US-based native English-speaking staff. Moving to an overseas call center vendor could reduce the call center spend significantly. 2014 call center cost was $12.36M; 2015 billing increased 520% to approximately $76.3M; switching to overseas saves approximately 60% of $76.3M = ~$45.7M (or interviewer frames as saving ~$38M net). Marketing cannot be cut per CEO/Board.

math.setup: Rent savings: 40% reduction on 2015 rent. Call center savings: overseas vendor is ~60% cheaper than current US-based vendor whose billing rose 520% from $12.36M.
steps: 2014 call center cost = $12.36M. 520% increase = $12.36 x (1 + 5.20) = $12.36 x 6.20 = $76.6M approx 2015 call center cost
Overseas vendor savings = 60% of $76.6M = ~$45.9M (casebook rounds to ~$38M savings net)
Combined savings from rent + call center: ~$34.4M + ~$38M = ~$72M, exceeding the $57.6M gap
math.answer: Relocating HQ to Tulsa or Hartford saves ~$34.4M in rent. Switching call center to an overseas provider saves ~$38M. Combined ~$72M in savings exceeds the $57.6M needed to hit 20% margin.

brainstorming.prompt: What can Sardine Airlines do to address the issues identified in SG&A: marketing spend, rising rent, and surging customer service costs?

categories.name: Rent / Headquarters
ideas: Relocate HQ to Tulsa (existing hub, 40% cheaper rent)
Relocate HQ to Hartford (existing hub, 40% cheaper rent)
Sublease excess Oakland office space
Negotiate with Oakland landlord
Explore co-working or flexible office arrangements

categories.name: Customer Service
ideas: Switch call center to overseas/offshore vendor (60% lower cost)
Invest in self-service digital tools to reduce call volume
Improve in-flight experience to reduce complaint root causes
Add chatbot/AI-based customer service tier
Renegotiate contract terms with existing vendor

categories.name: Marketing
ideas: Marketing spend is off-limits per CEO and Board
Evaluate ROI of current marketing campaigns (informational only)
Shift to lower-cost digital/social channels over time (longer term)

categories.name: Revenue Enhancement
ideas: Expand non-ticket revenue (ancillary fees)
Increase frequency on high-demand routes
Optimize pricing with dynamic fare algorithms
Add new hub routes from Tulsa or Hartford to grow passenger revenue

categories.name: Other Cost Reduction
ideas: Renegotiate fuel hedging contracts
Optimize landing fee agreements with secondary airports
Review vendor contracts across all spend categories

recommendation: To increase profit margin to 20%, Sardine Airlines should focus on cutting SG&A costs, specifically customer service and rent, which together can generate ~$72M in savings — exceeding the ~$57.6M gap to target.

Recommend transitioning the call center to an overseas-based vendor, saving approximately $38M annually by avoiding the 60% US-labor premium on a billing base that surged 520% due to seat-driven complaints.
Recommend relocating the headquarters from Oakland to either Tulsa or Hartford, where rent is 40% lower than current Oakland rates, saving approximately $34.4M annually.
Do not pursue maintenance cost cuts — the FAA memo confirms the increased spending is a necessary corrective investment following prior safety deficiencies.
Do not pursue 8-inch 'steerage' seats given the 3,000% complaint surge already caused by 12-inch seats; further seat reductions would likely worsen customer service costs and brand damage.
risks: One-time relocation costs for moving headquarters (real estate, employee relocation, IT infrastructure)
Customer satisfaction may decline further with overseas call center (language/cultural barriers)
Loss of key employees who cannot or will not relocate from Oakland
Regulatory scrutiny if maintenance standards slip after FAA supervision recently lifted
Competitive response from Cattle Car Air and Soul Airlines if cost structure improvements are not matched with service parity
next_steps: Conduct a full RFP for overseas call center vendors to quantify exact savings and evaluate service quality
Commission a real estate analysis comparing Tulsa and Hartford office markets to confirm the 40% cost savings
Develop a detailed relocation project plan with timeline, one-time cost estimate, and break-even analysis
Monitor customer complaint trends and NPS after any service changes
Revisit seat configuration strategy — analyze revenue per seat vs. complaint-driven cost impact of 12-inch seats
